case_name: Muhammad Nawaz vs. Province of Punjab
summary: In a dispute regarding inheritance of agricultural land between brothers, the Supreme Court held that entries in the revenue record carry presumption of truth under Section 42 of the Land Revenue Act. However, such presumption is rebuttable. The Court emphasized that oral gift (hiba) must be proved through clear evidence of declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession. Mutation alone is not conclusive proof of ownership.
key_holdings: Revenue record entries have presumption of truth but are rebuttable
Oral gift requires proof of declaration, acceptance and delivery of possession
Mutation is not a document of title
source: Sample Judgment for Demo (based on common SC principles)

case_name: Ghulam Qadir vs. Sh. Abdul Razzaq
summary: The Court clarified the principles of inheritance under Muslim Personal Law and Section 4 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. Children of a predeceased son/daughter are entitled to the share their parent would have received. The Court also held that a person in possession of property claiming ownership through inheritance must prove his claim with strong evidence when challenged.
key_holdings: Section 4 MFLO protects share of predeceased child's children
Burden of proof lies on the person asserting a particular share
Long standing possession can create strong presumption but not absolute title

case_name: Mst. Fatima Bibi vs. Muhammad Akram & others
summary: In a suit for declaration and permanent injunction regarding ancestral land, the Lahore High Court held that sisters cannot be deprived of their share in inheritance on the basis of alleged family settlement or oral gift unless the same is proved through reliable evidence. The Court directed mutation of shares according to Islamic law of inheritance.
key_holdings: Female heirs cannot be deprived of inheritance without clear proof of gift or relinquishment
Family settlement must be proved with clear evidence
Court can direct revenue authorities to correct mutation

summary: The Supreme Court reiterated that in cases of co-sharers (joint owners), one co-sharer cannot claim exclusive ownership without partition. A co-sharer in exclusive possession is not a trespasser vis-a-vis other co-sharers. Suit for possession by one co-sharer against another is not maintainable without seeking partition.
key_holdings: Co-sharer cannot claim exclusive title without partition
Exclusive possession by one co-sharer does not amount to ouster automatically
Proper remedy is suit for partition

case_name: Imran Khan vs. Federation of Pakistan (Property Rights)
summary: While dealing with property rights under Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, the Court held that the right to property is a fundamental right and any deprivation must strictly follow the procedure established by law. Arbitrary mutation or cancellation of mutation without notice violates principles of natural justice.
key_holdings: Right to property is fundamental under Articles 23 & 24
No person can be deprived of property without due process
Revenue authorities must follow principles of natural justice

case_name: Abdul Sattar vs. Mst. Zainab & Brothers
summary: In an inheritance dispute between brothers and sister over residential and agricultural property, the Court applied pure Islamic law of inheritance (Sunni Hanafi) and held that after the death of father, the property devolves upon all legal heirs according to their Quranic shares. Any alleged will exceeding one-third is invalid to the extent of excess without consent of heirs.
key_holdings: Islamic law of inheritance applies strictly
Will cannot exceed 1/3rd without consent of heirs
All legal heirs are entitled to their shares from the date of death
